questions.stem: Which group of atoms is present in every ester?
options: A -COO- group linking two hydrocarbon parts
A -COOH group at the end of a carbon chain
A -CONH- group linking two hydrocarbon parts
An -OH group attached to a saturated carbon
questions.explanation: Esters contain the -COO- group between two carbon chains, as in ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃. -COOH is a carboxylic acid and -CONH- is an amide link.

questions.stem: Which two classes of organic compound contain nitrogen?
options: Carboxylic acids and amines
Amines and amides
Esters and amides
Amines and alcohols
questions.explanation: Amines contain an amino group (-NH₂, or N bonded to other carbons) and amides contain the -CONH- group. Alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen.

questions.stem: Which of these compounds is an amine rather than an amide?
options: CH₃CH₂CONH₂
CH₃CH₂NH₂
CH₃CONH₂
HCONH₂
questions.explanation: In an amine the nitrogen is bonded to carbon and hydrogen only. In an amide the nitrogen is bonded to a carbonyl carbon, C=O, as in -CONH₂.

questions.stem: Which functional groups are present in HOCH₂CH₂NH₂?
options: An alcohol (hydroxyl) group and an amine (amino) group
A carboxylic acid group and an amide group
An alcohol (hydroxyl) group and an amide group
An ester group and an amine (amino) group
questions.explanation: HO- bonded to a saturated carbon is a hydroxyl group, and -NH₂ bonded to a carbon with no C=O is an amino group. There is no C=O, so there can be no acid, ester or amide group.

questions.stem: Propanoic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH) and methyl ethanoate (CH₃COOCH₃) both have the formula C₃H₆O₂. Which statement is correct?
options: They have different functional groups, so their chemical properties differ
They have the same functional group, so they react in exactly the same way
Methyl ethanoate is acidic, because it contains two oxygen atoms
Propanoic acid is an ester, because its molecule contains a C=O group
questions.explanation: These are structural isomers: one is a carboxylic acid and the other an ester. Only the acid donates a proton, for example fizzing with carbonates; containing oxygen or a C=O group does not make a compound acidic.

questions.stem: Four colourless liquids are each added to sodium carbonate solution. Only one gives bubbles of gas. Which liquid is it?
options: Ethanoic acid
Ethanol
Ethyl ethanoate
Butan-1-amine
questions.explanation: Carboxylic acids are proton donors and react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide. Alcohols and esters are neutral, and amines are bases, so none of them fizz with a carbonate.

questions.stem: A solution of an organic compound turns red litmus blue and reacts with hydrochloric acid to form a salt. To which class does it most likely belong?
options: Ester
Alcohol
Amine
Carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: The lone pair on an amine's nitrogen accepts a proton, so amines are weak bases that react with acids to form ammonium salts. Carboxylic acids would turn blue litmus red, and esters and alcohols are neutral.

questions.stem: Methanamine, CH₃NH₂, reacts with hydrochloric acid. What is the product?
options: Methylammonium chloride, CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻
Chloromethane and ammonia, CH₃Cl + NH₃
Methanol and ammonium chloride, CH₃OH + NH₄Cl
Methanamide and hydrogen, HCONH₂ + H₂
questions.explanation: This is an acid-base reaction: the amine's nitrogen accepts a proton to form the methylammonium ion, which pairs with chloride as an ionic salt. No carbon bonds are broken.

questions.stem: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium permanganate. What is observed, and what is the final organic product?
options: The orange colour turns green; propanoic acid forms
No colour change occurs; there is no reaction
The purple colour fades; propanoic acid forms
The purple colour fades; propanone forms
questions.explanation: A primary alcohol is oxidised, via the aldehyde, to a carboxylic acid, and purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colourless Mn²⁺. Propanone would come from propan-2-ol, and orange to green is the change seen with dichromate.

questions.stem: Which test result distinguishes 2-methylpropan-2-ol from butan-2-ol?
options: Only butan-2-ol turns hot acidified dichromate from orange to green
Only 2-methylpropan-2-ol turns hot acidified dichromate from orange to green
Only butan-2-ol fizzes when added to sodium carbonate solution
Only 2-methylpropan-2-ol turns red litmus paper blue in solution
questions.explanation: Butan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol and is oxidised to butanone, reducing orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ to green Cr³⁺. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary, with no hydrogen on the carbon bearing the -OH, so it is not oxidised. Neither alcohol is acidic or basic.

questions.stem: An alcohol is heated under reflux with excess acidified dichromate. The solution turns green, but the organic product does not fizz with sodium carbonate. What kind of alcohol was it?
options: A tertiary alcohol, which is not oxidised
A primary alcohol, oxidised to an ester
A secondary alcohol, oxidised to a ketone
A primary alcohol, oxidised to a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: The green colour shows the alcohol was oxidised, which rules out a tertiary alcohol. With excess oxidant a primary alcohol would form a carboxylic acid, which fizzes with carbonate; a ketone does not.

questions.stem: Which properties are typical of small ester molecules?
options: Sour taste and turning blue litmus paper red
Fishy smell and turning red litmus paper blue
Fizzing with carbonate to release carbon dioxide
Pleasant, fruity smells and no effect on litmus
questions.explanation: Small esters are neutral, volatile compounds with fruity odours, which is why they are used as flavours and perfumes. Sourness and fizzing with carbonates are acid properties, and a fishy smell is typical of amines.

questions.stem: Protein structure is described at several levels. Which level is the order of amino acids along the chain?
options: Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
Primary
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the order of amino acids in the chain. Secondary structure is local folding into α-helices and β-pleated sheets, and tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of the chain.

questions.stem: Silk is strong and stretches very little. Its protein consists largely of β-pleated sheets. What holds the strands of these sheets together?
options: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of the backbone
Peptide bonds between the R groups of neighbouring strands
Ionic bonds between the two ends of each protein chain
Disulfide bridges between every pair of amino acids
questions.explanation: In secondary structure, the C=O of one peptide group hydrogen bonds to the N-H of another. In β-sheets, many such bonds link extended strands side by side, giving silk its strength. Peptide bonds join amino acids along a chain, not between strands.

questions.stem: Which interactions are responsible for a protein's tertiary structure?
options: Peptide bonds between the amino group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of the next
Hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O and N-H groups only, forming helices and sheets
Glycosidic links between the sugar units attached along the length of the protein chain
Interactions between R groups: hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, disulfide bridges and dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Tertiary structure is the folding of the whole chain, held by interactions between the side chains (R groups) of amino acids that may be far apart in the sequence. Backbone hydrogen bonding alone gives secondary structure.

questions.stem: Hair contains the protein keratin, rich in the amino acid cysteine. A permanent wave treatment breaks one type of bond, the hair is reshaped, and the bonds reform in new positions. Which bonds?
options: Disulfide bridges between cysteine side chains
Peptide bonds along the protein backbone
Glycosidic links between keratin chains
Ester links between neighbouring chains
questions.explanation: Cysteine side chains form covalent S-S bridges that fix the tertiary structure of keratin. The treatment reduces these bridges, and after reshaping they are reformed in new positions. Breaking peptide bonds would destroy the protein chains.

questions.stem: When egg white is cooked, it changes from clear and runny to white and firm. What has happened to its proteins?
options: Their primary structure has changed, but the tertiary structure is unchanged
Their secondary and tertiary structures are disrupted; the primary structure is unchanged
Their peptide bonds have been broken, so the proteins have become free amino acids
New peptide bonds have formed between the chains, lengthening every protein
questions.explanation: Heat disrupts the hydrogen bonds and other interactions holding the folded shape, so the protein denatures and the unfolded chains tangle together. The covalent peptide bonds of the primary structure survive cooking.

questions.stem: Replacing a single amino acid in a protein can make it fold differently and lose its function. Which explanation is best?
options: A different R group changes the side-chain interactions that set the tertiary structure
A different amino acid breaks the peptide bonds on either side of it, splitting the chain
The change removes all of the hydrogen bonds from the protein's backbone
The change converts the protein into a carbohydrate, which has a different shape
questions.explanation: The primary structure determines how a chain folds, because the R groups decide which hydrogen bonds, ionic attractions, disulfide bridges and non-polar clusters form. Swapping one R group, for example a charged one for a non-polar one, can change the final shape.

questions.stem: Which monosaccharide is the monomer of starch, glycogen and cellulose?
options: Sucrose
Glycerol
Glucose
Fructose
questions.explanation: All three are polymers of glucose joined by glycosidic links; they differ in the form of glucose and the way the units are linked. Sucrose is a disaccharide and glycerol is not a sugar.

questions.stem: Cellulose forms strong, insoluble fibres in plant cell walls, but starch does not. What structural difference explains this?
options: Starch is held together by peptide bonds that water breaks, but cellulose has no peptide bonds at all
Cellulose chains are much shorter than starch chains, so they dissolve less readily and pack together
Cellulose has straight chains of β-glucose that hydrogen bond side by side; starch chains coil or branch
Cellulose is made of fructose units, which form stronger covalent links than the glucose units of starch
questions.explanation: The β-glycosidic links in cellulose give straight chains that lie parallel, with many hydrogen bonds between them, forming strong fibres. The α-links in starch make amylose coil into a helix and amylopectin branch, so the chains cannot pack as tightly.

questions.stem: Humans can digest starch but not cellulose, although both are made of glucose. Why?
options: Humans lack an enzyme that hydrolyses the β-glycosidic links in cellulose
Cellulose contains no glucose units once it has been cooked in food
Starch is a protein, so it is digested by enzymes that cellulose resists
Cellulose is too small to be recognised by human digestive enzymes
questions.explanation: Enzymes are specific to the shape of the link. Human amylase hydrolyses the α-links in starch, but humans make no cellulase to hydrolyse the β-links in cellulose, so it passes through as dietary fibre.

questions.stem: Glycogen, the energy store in animals, is more highly branched than the amylose in starch. Why is this branching useful?
options: It gives many chain ends, so glucose can be released quickly by enzymes
It makes the molecule straight, so the chains form strong structural fibres
It makes the molecule dissolve fully, so it can leave cells in the blood
It replaces glycosidic links with peptide bonds, which store more energy
questions.explanation: Enzymes remove glucose units from the ends of chains, and a highly branched molecule has many ends, so glucose can be released rapidly when needed, while the molecule stays compact for storage inside cells.

questions.stem: High-density polyethene (HDPE) is denser and stronger than low-density polyethene (LDPE), although both are made from ethene. Why?
options: HDPE is made from heavier ethene molecules, so each chain has a larger mass
HDPE chains have little branching, so they pack closely with stronger dispersion forces
HDPE chains are covalently cross-linked to each other, so they cannot move at all
HDPE chains contain oxygen atoms, which form hydrogen bonds between the chains
questions.explanation: Unbranched chains can line up closely, giving more contact between chains, stronger dispersion forces and higher density. LDPE's branches keep chains apart. Neither form is cross-linked or contains oxygen.

questions.stem: Why does a thermosetting polymer char rather than melt when it is heated strongly?
options: It contains no carbon in its chains, so it cannot soften as plastics do
Its chains are very short, so it decomposes before the chains can move
Covalent cross-links join its chains, so they cannot slide past each other
Only weak dispersion forces hold its chains, so they break apart at once
questions.explanation: In a thermoset, strong covalent bonds link the chains into a network, so heating breaks bonds and decomposes the material instead of letting chains move. Thermoplastics have only intermolecular forces between chains, so they soften and melt.

questions.stem: Why does polylactic acid (PLA), a polyester, biodegrade more readily than polyethene?
options: PLA is much denser than polyethene, so microorganisms can absorb it whole
PLA's ester links can be hydrolysed; polyethene has only C-C and C-H bonds
PLA is an addition polymer, and addition polymers always break down quickly
Polyethene is a condensation polymer whose amide links resist all enzymes
questions.explanation: Ester links in the PLA backbone can be broken by water and microbial enzymes, splitting the chain into small molecules. Polyethene, an addition polymer, has a backbone of strong, non-polar C-C bonds that few organisms can attack.

questions.stem: Nylon and Kevlar are polyamides that form very strong fibres. Which interaction between chains is mainly responsible?
options: Ionic bonds between positive and negative ions spaced along neighbouring chains
Disulfide bridges between sulfur atoms in the side chains of neighbouring chains
Glycosidic links between ring structures on neighbouring polymer chains
Hydrogen bonds between N-H and C=O groups of amide links on neighbouring chains
questions.explanation: Each amide link has an N-H and a C=O, so aligned chains form many hydrogen bonds with each other. In Kevlar the rigid, straight chains line up especially well, giving great strength.

questions.stem: Apart from tiny isotope peaks, the highest m/z peak in the mass spectrum of an organic compound is at 46. What does this show?
options: The compound has a boiling point of 46 °C
The compound has a relative molecular mass of 46
The most abundant fragment ion has a mass of 46
The compound contains 46 atoms in each molecule
questions.explanation: The molecular ion, M⁺, is the whole molecule with one electron removed, so it appears at the highest m/z and gives the molecular mass. The most abundant ion gives the base peak, which is often a fragment.

questions.stem: What is the base peak in a mass spectrum?
options: The peak at the lowest m/z, produced by the smallest possible fragment ion
The peak produced by ions of the carbon-12 standard used to calibrate the machine
The tallest peak, from the most abundant ion, given a relative intensity of 100
The peak at the highest m/z, produced by the molecular ion of the compound
questions.explanation: Peak heights are scaled relative to the tallest, the base peak, from the most stable or abundant ion. It may or may not be the molecular ion.

questions.stem: A mass spectrum shows the molecular ion at m/z 58 and a large peak at m/z 43. Which group was most likely lost to form the m/z 43 ion?
options: OH, mass 17
CO, mass 28
CH₃, mass 15
C₂H₅, mass 29
questions.explanation: 58 - 43 = 15, the mass of a methyl group. Butane, for example, gives C₃H₇⁺ at m/z 43 by losing CH₃; losing C₂H₅ would leave a peak at m/z 29.

questions.stem: The mass spectrum of chloroethane, C₂H₅Cl, has two molecular ion peaks, at m/z 64 and 66, with heights in a ratio of about 3 : 1. Why?
options: Chloroethane breaks into two fragments that differ by two hydrogen atoms
Carbon-13 makes up about a quarter of the carbon atoms in the sample
Some molecules gain two extra electrons when they pass through the ioniser
Chlorine exists naturally as ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl in roughly a 3 : 1 ratio
questions.explanation: Molecules containing ³⁵Cl give M⁺ at 24 + 5 + 35 = 64 and those with ³⁷Cl at 66, in proportion to the isotopes' abundances. Carbon-13 is only about 1% of carbon, so it gives a very small M+1 peak.

questions.stem: What does an infrared (IR) spectrum mainly reveal about an organic compound?
options: The relative molecular mass of the compound
The exact positions of all atoms in three dimensions
The number of carbon atoms in each molecule
The types of bonds and functional groups present
questions.explanation: Bonds absorb infrared radiation at characteristic wavenumbers as they vibrate, so absorption bands identify groups such as O-H, N-H and C=O. Mass spectrometry gives molecular mass and X-ray crystallography gives three-dimensional positions.

questions.stem: An IR spectrum shows a strong absorption at about 1740 cm⁻¹ (C=O) but no absorption between 2500 and 3600 cm⁻¹ apart from C-H near 2900 cm⁻¹. To which class does the compound most likely belong?
options: Carboxylic acid
Alcohol
Amine
Ester
questions.explanation: A C=O absorption with no O-H or N-H band fits an ester. A carboxylic acid would also show a very broad O-H band, an alcohol a broad O-H band without C=O, and an amine an N-H band.

questions.stem: A compound's molecular ion is at m/z 60. Its IR spectrum shows a very broad absorption at 2500-3300 cm⁻¹ (O-H, acid) and a strong absorption near 1710 cm⁻¹ (C=O). Which compound is it?
options: Methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃
Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH
Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
questions.explanation: All four have a molecular mass of 60, so mass spectrometry alone cannot decide. The IR spectrum shows both an acid O-H and a C=O, which only ethanoic acid has; the alcohols lack C=O and the ester lacks O-H.

questions.stem: Propanamide and propan-1-amine both show N-H absorptions at about 3300-3500 cm⁻¹. Which absorption appears only in the spectrum of propanamide?
options: A sharp C≡N absorption at about 2250 cm⁻¹
A strong C=O absorption at about 1650-1700 cm⁻¹
A broad O-H absorption at about 3200-3600 cm⁻¹
A C-H absorption at about 2850-3000 cm⁻¹
questions.explanation: The amide group, -CONH₂, contains a carbonyl, so propanamide shows a strong C=O band; propan-1-amine has no C=O. Both compounds have C-H bonds, and neither contains O-H or C≡N.

questions.stem: What information does X-ray crystallography give about a molecule?
options: Only the functional groups present, from the wavenumbers that are absorbed
The colour of light it absorbs, which identifies the elements it contains
The three-dimensional positions of its atoms, including bond lengths and angles
Its relative molecular mass and the masses of the fragments it breaks into
questions.explanation: X-rays diffracted by a crystal produce a pattern from which an electron density map, and so the positions of the atoms, can be calculated. It has been used to find the structures of DNA, proteins and many medicines.

questions.stem: What form must a sample be in for X-ray crystallography, and why?
options: A dilute solution, so the molecules can rotate freely and show all of their faces
A fine powder burned in a flame, so the atoms emit X-rays of their own characteristic energy
A well-ordered crystal, so the regular array of molecules gives a clear diffraction pattern
A gas at low pressure, so the molecules are far apart and do not scatter each other's X-rays
questions.explanation: The method depends on X-rays scattering from many identical molecules repeated in a regular lattice, which reinforces the scattered waves into a measurable pattern. Growing a suitable crystal, for example of a protein, is often the hardest step.

questions.stem: Why are hydrogen atoms the hardest atoms to locate in a structure found by X-ray crystallography?
options: Hydrogen atoms are too heavy to scatter X-rays as other atoms do
Hydrogen atoms absorb all of the X-rays, so they leave no pattern
Hydrogen atoms vibrate only at infrared frequencies, not X-ray ones
X-rays are scattered by electrons, and a hydrogen atom has only one
questions.explanation: The diffraction pattern maps electron density. Atoms with many electrons scatter strongly, but hydrogen, with a single electron often pulled towards its bonding partner, scatters weakly and is hard to place.

questions.stem: A chemist needs the molecular mass, the functional groups and the full three-dimensional structure of a new crystalline compound. Which techniques, in that order, provide each?
options: Infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, X-ray crystallography
X-ray crystallography, infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry
Mass spectrometry, X-ray crystallography, infrared spectroscopy
Mass spectrometry, infrared spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography
questions.explanation: The molecular ion in a mass spectrum gives the molecular mass, IR absorptions identify functional groups, and X-ray diffraction from a crystal gives atomic positions. Structures are usually confirmed using evidence from several techniques together.
